summary:
We developed a web application that analyzes historical fire trends and predicts future trends. We harmonized NASA's archived data to ensure MODIS and VIIRS data differences were accounted for. Our application is intended to aid first responders and those living in high-risk areas.

Our application displays the harmonized data in an intuitive way using graphs and other visual elements.
details:
Languages/Tools:
Astro, TypeScript, SQL, Motherduck DB, Mapbox, Python, and everything is hosted on Vercel. The database has 56 million rows and is stored on DuckDB on Motherduck. Questions are answered by Gemma 4 31B running in OLLAMA.

What It Does/How it works:
There a clickable globe. For every place you click, data for 100 mile radius around the clicked point is loaded. There are five primary graphical representations of the data, including: a yearly calendar, a weekly calendar, a trend graph, a season drift graph, and a comparison of the two different sensors used to gather the data.

The data comes from the NASA FIRMS historical archive. MODIS covers data from 2000 to 2026, and VIIRS covers data starting from 2012. Latitude and Longitude are sent to a query, and the database returns the weeks a fire burned. VIIRS is an upgraded sensor that is best suited for small fires, while MODIS covers a larger radius and is better for large fires. The data was harmonized without overlap.


Purpose/Impact:
Our team grew up in California, so we know first hand the impact fires can have on families. The intended purpose of our project is to help first responders and individuals alike respond to fires quickly to help avoid injury and even death. We wanted to create a website where users can access satellite data from the last twenty-five years in a way that is easy to understand.
